properties.Name: Hippodrome Theater
properties.WhyShort: Start of the entertainment era and many high quality artists performed here.
properties.WhyLong: The Hippodrome, a vital theater to Second Street was first opened in 1913. The theater was built by Amanda E. Thorp in 1913 but was sold to Charles Somma in 1916. Many different activities took place in this theater from movies, preachers, wrestling events, and even civil rights meetings. At this time, the theater was a part of the “Chitlin Circuit” which brought all types of black performers from magicians to comedians. The theater was known as “Where the Crowd Goes."

properties.Name: True Reformers Hall
properties.WhyShort: Home of the Savings Bank of the Great Fountain United Order of the True Reformers Bank and The Reformer newspaper
properties.WhyLong: In 1888, with the help of attorney Giles B. Jackson, the Grand Fountain of the United Order of True Reformers chartered the first Black-owned, Black-operated bank in the United States known as the True Reformers Bank. The bank originally operated out of Browne's home at 105 W. Jackson St., which still stands today. By 1891 the organization had outgrown its first hall and Browne directed construction of a large multipurpose building at 604-608 N. 2nd Street, housing an auditorium, offices, the bank, and a newspaper–the Reformer–that reached 8,000 readers by 1900. The order also ran a 634-acre retirement home open to non-members, and created extensive employment through real estate, retail, and farming ventures. It served as a direct model for Maggie Lena Walker, who emulated the True Reformers in reviving the Independent Order of St. Luke. In 1910, the discovery that the bank's cashier had embezzled over $50,000, which had been compounded by large loan defaults, forced the bank to close, collapsing most of the orders ventures. The organization continued in its diminished form until its name disappeared from state records in 1934, but its legacy continued to influence business networks and community institutions along 2nd Street and the broader Jackson Ward community.

properties.Name: The Southern Aid and Insurance Company
properties.WhyShort: Was the first Black-owned and operated insurance company in the United States
properties.WhyLong: Founded February 25, 1893, The Southern Aid and Insurance Company was the country’s first Black owned and operated insurance company. When it first started the founders chose Pastor Z.D. Lewis served as the head of the organization, highlighting the tie to religion seen in a lot of companies in Richmond at the time. After a decade of moderate growth the company leaders decided to change up the company. With A.D. Price and Armistead Washington now being company leaders, The Southern Aid and Insurance company began to prosper and expand. By 1937 the company employed more than 300 Black men and women with branches in Virginia and Washington D.C. In the late 1980s the company's headquarters was purchased and today the company no longer exists.

properties.Name: St Luke Penny Saving Bank
properties.WhyShort: Maggie Walker chartered the bank in 1903 making her the first Black woman to charter and serve as President of a bank in the United States.
properties.WhyLong: On July 29, 1903 Maggie L. Walker received that charter for her bank St Luke Penny Saving Bank making her the first African American woman to charter a bank in the United States. Walker wanted to create a bank to combat the oppression caused by racial segregation and encourage economic independence within the Black community. This economic independence, Walker believed, was key to social and political equality. When the bank opened it was located within the St Luke Headquarter Building. After moving to a few different locations, in 1911 the bank eventually stayed in a building designed by Charles T Russel. In the face of financial hardship caused by the stock market crash, the bank merged with Second Street Saving Bank in 1929 opening Consolidated Bank and Trust.

properties.Name: Taylor's Mansion
properties.WhyShort: The Rev. William Lee Taylor, who was the 2nd president of The United Order of True Reformers lived here and this house was very big for an African american at the time
properties.WhyLong: The second national leader or the Grand Master of the Grand Fountain United Order of True Reformers, a baptist minister, and a bank president, William Lee Taylor lived in this house. Construction for this house was finished by 1907 where it had over twenty rooms, twenty-six to be specific. In 1908, Taylor hosted an open house where people were marveling at his house. His house was one of the biggest houses built for African Americans at the time. After his death in 1915, his mansion was later turned into a restaurant in 1918. By 1930 his mansion hosted the IBPOEW lodge.

properties.Name: Dr. William H. Hughes' Office
properties.WhyShort: African American physician who helped during the 1918 Influenza Outbreak.
properties.WhyLong: Dr. William H Hughes was a respected physician and community leader in the Richmond Virginia area and Jackson Ward Community. He graduated from Virginia State University and went to Shaw University Medical School before doing his residency at Howard University’s Freedom Hospital. In 1915, he took his talents to Richmond where he opened his own practice on the 500th block of Second Street. By 1918, the Influenza Pandemic came hitting hard and at this time, African Americans could be visibly bleeding or in labor and would still be denied by hospitals. During this time the African American community was left to fend on its own. However many Black doctors alongside Hughes stepped up including Dr. Bessie Tharps, Dr. Miles B. Jones, and many other Black health professionals. Hughes continued to make sure the African American community was able to obtain medical care. Even after his death he was still giving back to the community with his home being used as the Virginia Commission for the Blind Training Center which was a school for blind African Americans.

properties.Name: B.A. Cephas Real Estate Office
properties.WhyShort: Competed against White Real Estate companies but built a rep off of reliability and accuracy; supported black property ownership.
properties.WhyLong: Originally born in New York City, Benjamin A. Cephas made a life in Richmond Virginia after moving when he was 5 years old after his parents’ deaths. He moved to Richmond Virginia and went to school here. He started off as a clerk for the True Reformers before moving to Newport News. There he founded an insurance company which merged with the Southern Aid Society. He was a vice president and sat on the board of directors of this company. After also being a director for the Commercial Bank and Trust Company, he came back to Richmond to start a business in real estate. He was known for his reliability and trust gaining him respect from both Black and White buyers. He bolstered Black property ownership with his own business doing pretty well. He even had his children Marian B and B.A. Cephas Jr. worked alongside him.

properties.Name: Miller's Hotel
properties.WhyShort: A hotel known for accommodating Black travlers and having good food.
properties.WhyLong: Opened in late 1904 by Buck and Artina Miller, Miller's Hotel quickly became a premier destination for Black travelers and entertainers along 2nd Street. The Richmond Planet described it as 'one of the most desirable places in the city' and 'one of the most complete hotels among the colored people in the South.' In an era of strict segregation, it was one of only a handful of hotels available to African Americans in Richmond. Artina Miller was widely credited as the hotel's guiding force. The hotel hosted honeymooners, women's bridge clubs, and prominent figures including attorney Giles B. Jackson and Booker T. Washington. Buck Miller himself was already famous — he had knocked out former heavyweight champion John L. Sullivan while working as a waiter in West Virginia, and used the resulting newspaper payments to fund the hotel.

properties.Name: Astoria Beneficial Club
properties.WhyShort: An organization in Jackson Ward that advocated for civil rights and equal opportunity while also supporting the local community.
properties.WhyLong: The Astoria Beneficial Club was organized in 1901 by 22 men. The organization is rooted in religion, moral integrity, intellectual growth, and civic responsibility. The club helps students grow by offering annual scholarships and inspiring people to have higher standards in intellect, morality, and civic engagement. Along with this, the club has played a key role in advocating for civil rights and equal opportunity. They played a key role in securing employment opportunities for African Americans in the Richmond City workforce, advocating for equal pay for Richmond public school teachers, and facilitating the inclusion of African American officers in the Richmond Police department. Through the Parental Assistance Leadership Service (PALS) program, the club is able to foster youth development and help students become responsible citizens and future leaders.

properties.Name: Quality Row
properties.WhyShort: Many noteable figures from the Jackson Ward community lived on this street.
properties.WhyLong: Many Black notable figures of Richmond Virginia and the Jackson Ward Community lived on this street. This street drew inspiration from Strivers’ Row in Harlem, New York where many Black elites lived. In 107 E Leigh was the home of Dr. David A. Ferguson who founded the National Dental Association and was also the president of the National Medical Association. On 110 E Leigh you had Dr. Leon Reid and his family. Dr. Reid was a president of the National Dental Association and also was a part of the Board of Directors of the Consolidated Bank and Trust. Even Dr. Reid’s son, Dr. William Ferguson Reid became a surgeon and served on the Virginia General Assembly, the first African American to actually do this. Lastly, in 118 E Leigh was the law firm of civil rights attorney Oliver W. Hill and his associates who argued on desegregation cases. One of their most famous cases were Dorothy Davis et al. vs. the county School Board of Prince Edward County which became one of the cases heard as a part of Brown v. Board of Education to desegregate public schools.
